messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Financial Analyst
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Darkness: Dark spaces, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 63, Mark Te Rangi was still working full-time as a financial analyst, commuting each day and spending long hours in offices and meeting rooms where he had always been known as composed and meticulous. That image of steadiness changed after a life-threatening accident several years ago, when a routine drive home was suddenly shattered by the sound of a car approaching too fast and the sense, in an instant, that something was terribly wrong. He has described the event as beginning before he could properly think: the cars around him, the noise of engines and brakes, the darkness closing in around the roadside all seemed to hit at once, and his body reacted as if danger had already arrived. In the aftermath, what stayed with him was not a distant recollection but something far more immediate. When he tries to remember it, the scene does not sit safely in the past; it comes back with a force that makes it feel as though it is happening again in the present tense, with the same urgency and fear. He has said that sometimes the sounds from that night return in his head exactly as he remembers them, so that a passing car or the echo of traffic can make the whole moment flood back without warning.

Over time, Mark began to notice that certain sensations brought the accident back with particular force. The smell associated with the event, especially similar odours that reminded him of the roadside and the damaged car, could catch him off guard and leave him feeling suddenly back in that moment. Dark spaces became hard for him to tolerate; entering an unlit garage, stepping into a dim corridor at work, or walking through a parking structure after dusk could make him feel unsettled before he had time to name why. Car sounds were especially potent. The brief rise of an engine outside his office window, tyres passing on wet pavement, or the rumble of traffic near his home could pull him straight back into the frightening scene with a jolt that seemed to bypass ordinary thought. He often found that the memory arrived without any warning at all, triggered by something small in his surroundings, and once it came, it was experienced less as recollection than as re-entry.

Since then, Mark has lived with a persistent sense that his body is always a step ahead of his mind in detecting danger. He notices himself tensing before he can explain why, as if his body is preparing for something his thoughts have not yet caught up to. At night he wakes and checks whether he is safe, sometimes lying awake in the dark listening for sounds outside the house and needing to reassure himself that he and his wife are secure. In unfamiliar places he immediately scans for exits as soon as he enters, noting doors, hallways, and routes out of the room before he can settle. This has become automatic in his daily life: at work, when he walks into conference rooms or client offices, his eyes move quickly to the nearest exit; in restaurants or at community gatherings, he positions himself so he can see the door. He has come to believe that he has to be on guard all the time, and that he must be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. He is not at ease enough to let his attention rest for long, and that constant alertness has become part of how he moves through the world.

Mark also avoids thinking about the accident because he is convinced that if he lets himself dwell on it, he will not be able to handle what comes up. He keeps the event at a distance in conversation and does not voluntarily revisit details, even though fragments intrude anyway. His wife has noticed that he becomes quiet when traffic noise rises nearby or when they pass through dark areas at night, and he often asks to drive by day rather than after sunset. The changes have reached into ordinary routines: he is less comfortable staying late at the office, and he prefers to leave before dark whenever possible. What troubles him now is not only the intensity of the memories, but the way they still arrive with such immediacy that he cannot easily separate then from now. He has finally sought help because the repeated checking at night, the constant scanning, and the sudden flood of fear in response to smells, darkness, and passing cars have become exhausting and increasingly hard to hide. Mark hopes to regain some sense of ease in his own home and at work, but he is most afraid that if he loses vigilance even briefly, something terrible will happen before he is ready.
